before: A study-log pipeline can parse a string, reject invalid domain values and keep a finite number of accepted entries. Integer(text, 10, exception: false) returns nil for invalid decimal text instead of raising; range cover? checks the inclusive 1..60 domain.

next skips invalid input; break stops once two valid entries have been accepted. Array << appends and sum adds the accepted integers. This tiny finite input does not establish streaming size limits, persistence or a complete import-error reporting policy.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
input = ["15", "bad", "0", "20"]
accepted = []
input.each do |text|
  value = Integer(text, 10, exception: false)
  next unless value && (1..60).cover?(value)
  accepted << value
  break if accepted.length == 2
end
p accepted
puts accepted.sum

```

Expected output or behavior: [15, 20]
35. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Explain the difference between limiting accepted entries and limiting total input bytes. You may trace it without a Ruby interpreter; reading completion is not proof of a local run.

Bad text and numbers outside one through sixty do not use a place.

Follow the labeled parts of this example.
```ruby
input = ["15", "bad", "0", "20"]
accepted = []
input.each do |text|

  next unless value && (1..60).cover?(value)
  accepted << value
  break if accepted.length == 2
end
p accepted
puts accepted.sum
```
The output is `[15, 20]`, then `35`. Fifteen and twenty are accepted. They add to thirty-five.

before.question: If the first input changes from 15 to 70, what remains?
before.explanation: 70 exceeds the upper bound, bad is not an integer and zero is below the lower bound; only 20 is accepted.

after.question: What stays if seventy replaces fifteen?
after.explanation: Seventy is too large. Twenty is the only valid time left.
